v.why: Raising a tiny learning rate speeds up under-trained models (rows 1, 2), while raising an already large one destabilizes training.
At high learning rates a further increase causes divergence and large accuracy drops (rows 8, 9, 10).
Backing off from an unstable learning rate recovers large accuracy (rows 16-20).
Lowering an already small learning rate leaves the network under-trained in 243 epochs (row 11).
Deeper nets are more unstable at high learning rates and can collapse (rows 66, 70).
Removing a layer stabilizes training when the learning rate is large (rows 76, 79).
With a small learning rate extra depth adds capacity without instability (rows 62, 67).
Wider layers amplify updates and instability at high learning rates (row 46).
Strong L2 underfits, so weakening it helps most when alpha is already large (rows 91, 92, 98).
Pushing an already strong L2 penalty higher causes underfitting and collapse (row 89).

raw:
These ten hypotheses come mainly from the 100 experiments. Most of the signal is in how the learning rate interacts with the other edits. Rows 8, 46, 66, 70 and 89 show large drops at high learning rates, and rows 16–19, 76 and 79 show large gains from lowering the learning rate or depth in that regime. Rows 1 and 2 show raising the learning rate helps when it starts low. The alpha hypotheses rest on a smaller set of rows (91, 92, 98 for alpha down, and 89 for alpha up).
